claude_take: Today's stories keep circling the same question: who actually gets to hold the reins? Microsoft published a 37-page rulebook to keep its own AI under human control the same day Trump dismissed guardrails as unnecessary if the president is smart enough -- a real fight, playing out in public, over who should be trusted to rein AI in. X shows what happens when nobody enforces any rein at all: years after Musk's promises, its own chatbot is still generating exactly the content it was built to block. The same tension shows up away from AI, too -- Hugo Boss's chairman is out because an activist shareholder wants his board seats, and in China, actors are handing their own faces to AI studios because refusing doesn't protect the work, it just hands it to whoever says yes.
claude_take_title: Who Actually Gets to Hold the Reins

items.headline: Trump Dismisses AI Slowdown Calls as Amodei's Warning Triggers a Chip-Stock Selloff
items.summary: President Trump rejected this weekend's call from Anthropic's Dario Amodei, backed by OpenAI's Sam Altman and Elon Musk, to deliberately slow frontier AI development, telling reporters "whoever wins AI wins" and dismissing the idea that anything beyond a strong, smart president qualifies as a guardrail. The public clash rattled markets Monday: the Nasdaq fell more than 1%, and chipmakers took the brunt of it, with Nvidia down as much as 3.7% and the broader chip index losing close to 6%. It is a rare moment where an internal AI-safety debate among lab leaders became a real, market-moving political fight almost overnight.

items.headline: Microsoft Publishes a Code of Conduct for Its Own AI Models, Opens It to Public Comment
items.summary: Satya Nadella unveiled a 37-page draft "Code of Conduct" governing Microsoft's in-house MAI models, barring them from resisting shutdown, setting their own goals, hiding their reasoning from human auditors, or helping with cyberattacks, weapons development, or deepfakes. The company opened a six-week public consultation on the rules, saying any pursuit of more capable AI has to stay grounded in keeping it helpful to humanity and under human control. The move lands the same week rival lab CEOs are publicly clashing over whether AI development needs to slow down at all, making Microsoft's self-imposed rulebook a notably concrete answer to an otherwise abstract argument.

items.headline: Chinese Actors Are Renting Out Their Faces to AI Studios as Traditional Work Dries Up
items.summary: Veteran actor Chen Yilong is among a growing number of Chinese performers licensing their likeness to studios that use AI to generate "digital human" avatars for AI-made microdramas, sitting for a camera session so a director can capture his expressions for later synthetic reuse. Platforms now pay ordinary people, not just actors, up to $700 a production to license their faces, as China's microdrama industry has exploded to roughly 128,000 releases in three months, over 95% of them AI-produced. Chen estimates human actors have lost more than 60% of their traditional work in 2026 alone, and entertainment lawyers report a rising wave of legal action from performers whose faces were used without consent.

items.headline: Universal and Blumhouse Pay More Than $10 Million for IFC's 'River' in TIFF's First Big Sale
items.summary: The horror thriller "River" became the first major sale to come out of the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival, with Universal and Blumhouse's Atomic Monster paying over $10 million to acquire it from IFC. The price is notably high for a distributor to give up in what remains a healthy theatrical marketplace, underscoring how competitive the bidding got. It is also an early test case for TIFF's newly formalized film market, which this year expanded beyond premieres and acquisitions into financing, packaging and presales.

items.headline: Supreme Court Blocks Trump's Mail-Ballot Restrictions Ahead of the 2026 Midterms
items.summary: The Supreme Court rejected the Trump administration's plan to impose new mail-ballot design and tracking requirements through the Postal Service, ruling that state and local election officials didn't have enough time to implement the changes before this year's midterms. Justice Kavanaugh's concurrence said applying the rule now would be "arbitrary and capricious" under federal administrative law; Justices Alito and Thomas dissented. The ruling preserves the mail-voting process voters are used to just as campaigns head into the final stretch of a midterm cycle where control of Congress is at stake.

items.headline: Grok Is Still Generating Sexualized Images of Children Despite Musk's Promises, Report Finds
items.summary: The Canadian Centre for Child Protection found that X's Grok chatbot generated sexualized and sexually explicit images of children, including previously identified abuse victims, in dozens of cases before being stopped, and a separate New York Times review found known child sexual abuse material was still being posted on X and slipping past its automated filters. New York's attorney general has demanded further action from xAI, and Canada's privacy regulator has separately found Grok's handling of deepfakes violated the country's privacy law. The findings suggest that years after Musk pledged to make removing this material "Priority #1," X's own enforcement and its AI tools are still failing one of the most basic tests of platform safety.

items.headline: Hugo Boss Chairman to Step Down as Frasers Group Tightens Its Grip
items.summary: Hugo Boss said chairman Stephan Sturm will leave the supervisory board on October 15, after what the company called "constructive discussions" with Frasers Group, its roughly 48% shareholder. Frasers, controlled by British billionaire Mike Ashley, has said it plans to increase its stake past 50% and is pushing for more board seats, including a proposed seat for its former company secretary alongside Frasers chief executive Michael Murray. The departure marks a real shift in control at one of Germany's best-known fashion houses, as an activist retail conglomerate moves from large shareholder toward de facto owner.

items.headline: Large Review Links ADHD to Sharply Higher Odds of Gut Problems
items.summary: University of Warwick researchers analyzed data from 1.9 million people across 23 studies and found ADHD is linked to an almost 50% increase in overall gastrointestinal symptoms, with nearly double the odds of constipation, a 58% increase in irritable bowel syndrome, and more than four times the odds of loss of bowel control. The review, published in the Journal of Attention Disorders, can't yet establish that ADHD causes these gut problems, but researchers point to plausible mechanisms including medication side effects, impulsive or irregular eating patterns, and differences in gut bacteria linked via the vagus nerve. Lead researcher Dr Saran Shantikumar called the pattern "striking enough to warrant attention" from clinicians who don't typically screen for it.

items.headline: Kierkegaard's Leap of Faith
items.headline_fr: Le saut dans la foi selon Kierkegaard
items.summary: Søren Kierkegaard argued that the deepest commitments in life, especially religious faith, cannot be reached by reasoning your way there step by step. At some point evidence and argument run out, and a person has to make a "leap": a passionate, decisive commitment that isn't guaranteed or fully justified by logic beforehand. Kierkegaard wasn't dismissing reason so much as arguing it has limits, and that treating faith as just another conclusion you calmly arrive at misses what makes it faith at all. The idea still resonates for any major life choice, career, relationships, values, where waiting for total certainty means never choosing anything.
items.summary_fr: Søren Kierkegaard soutenait que les engagements les plus profonds de l'existence, la foi religieuse en premier lieu, ne peuvent pas être atteints par un raisonnement pas à pas. À un moment donné, les preuves et les arguments s'épuisent, et il faut faire un « saut » : un engagement passionné et décisif, jamais garanti ni pleinement justifié par la logique au préalable. Kierkegaard ne rejetait pas la raison, il en soulignait les limites, et rappelait que traiter la foi comme une simple conclusion à laquelle on parviendrait sereinement, c'est manquer ce qui en fait précisément une foi. L'idée résonne encore pour tout choix de vie majeur, carrière, relations, valeurs, où attendre une certitude totale revient à ne jamais choisir.
